author: DailyMail
title: UK School Heatwave Closures Spark Debate on Resilience and Working Parents
text:
Over 1,000 UK schools close due to extreme heat, igniting discussion about unintended consequences such as increased parental strain, gender inequality in childcare, and the erosion of children's resilience amid rising school refusal rates.
Earlier this week, a wave of complaints spread across the United Kingdom as parents received sudden notifications that their children's schools would be closing due to extreme heat.
The country is experiencing a significant heatwave, with temperatures climbing into the high 20s Celsius. In response, more than 1,000 schools have opted to shut their doors or reduce operating hours. This decision has thrown countless family routines into disarray, particularly affecting working parents who must now arrange emergency childcare. The burden often falls disproportionately on mothers, who are more likely to adjust their work schedules or take unexpected leave.
A friend single-handedly managing her career and childcare described being forced to drop her son at her parents' house in the suburbs, then endure a delayed, crowded train to arrive late at her office. Her male boss, who has a wife and a nanny, expressed little sympathy, highlighting a persistent gender gap in domestic responsibilities. Another mother in Surrey has been forced to use her holiday days to stay home, ironically longing for the office air conditioning.
A colleague reports that her daughter's private school introduced optional half days, which in practice are mandatory and deeply inconvenient for full-time working parents. The schools justify these measures by citing a duty to prioritise pupil and staff wellbeing. But does closing schools truly safeguard wellbeing? While extreme heat poses risks, most children are healthy and can manage with simple precautions like water bottles, sunscreen, and cheap handheld fans.
Closing classrooms may inadvertently reduce resilience and create a generation less able to cope with normal life challenges. Moreover, school often provides a safe, supervised environment; in France, where similar temperatures are being experienced, 40 people have drowned in unsupervised swimming spots this week, many of them young people. Another critical concern is the issue of school refusal, or Emotionally-Based School Avoidance (ESBA).
Recent data reveals 176,361 pupils were severely absent (missing over 50 percent of classes) in the 2024/25 school year, a 193 percent rise since before the pandemic. Lockdowns increased childhood anxiety and diminished coping skills, creating a perfect storm. With an underfunded, overstretched CAMHS, this problem is worsening. Parents of children already struggling with attendance fear that these closures will reinforce the message that school is optional, making it even harder to re-establish routines.
The closures send a powerful signal: formal education is fragile, and comfort trumps commitment. This raises questions about societal priorities and whether we are adequately equipping the next generation to handle adversity, or instead, coddling them at the cost of their long-term development and mental fortitude
